q: What is a language model?
short: A model that assigns a probability to a sequence of words, P(w₁…wₙ), or equivalently to the next word given the history, P(wₙ | w₁…wₙ₋₁).
example: P(I saw a van) ≫ P(eyes awe of an).
follow: How is it used in speech recognition?
mistakes: Confusing it with a classifier of whole documents.

q: State the Markov assumption for a bigram model.
short: The probability of a word depends only on the previous word: P(wₖ | w₁…wₖ₋₁) ≈ P(wₖ | wₖ₋₁).
example: P(transparent | its water is so) ≈ P(transparent | so).

q: Compute P(am | I) and P(Sam | <s>) for 'I am Sam / Sam I am / I do not like green eggs and ham'.
short: P(am | I) = C(I am)/C(I) = 2/3; P(Sam | <s>) = 1/3.

q: Why use log probabilities?
short: Multiplying many probabilities below 1 underflows floating point; adding logs is stable and faster, and exponentiating at the end recovers the probability.

q: What is the zero-count problem?
short: Any n-gram not in the training data gets MLE probability 0, so any test sentence containing it gets probability 0 and perplexity becomes infinite, although the phrase may be perfectly normal.
mistakes: Assuming more data removes all zeros.

q: Write add-1 smoothing for bigrams.
short: P(wₙ | wₙ₋₁) = (C(wₙ₋₁wₙ) + 1)/(C(wₙ₋₁) + V), with V the vocabulary size.

q: Backoff vs interpolation?
short: Backoff uses the highest-order n-gram with enough evidence, switching to lower orders only when needed; interpolation always mixes all orders with weights λ that sum to 1.

q: What is perplexity?
short: PP(W) = P(w₁…w_N)^(−1/N): inverse test-set probability normalised by length, equal to the average branching factor; lower is better.

q: Compute P(<s> i want english food </s>) given .25, .33, .0011, .5, .68.
C(i want) = 827, C(i) = 2533, V = 1446: give add-1 P and the reconstituted count.
short: P = 828/3979 ≈ 0.208; c* = 828 × 2533/3979 ≈ 527, so add-1 removed about 300 counts of mass from this frequent pair.

q: How do you tune interpolation weights?
short: Fix counts from training data, then choose λs (possibly context-dependent) to maximise the likelihood of a separate held-out set, for example by grid search or EM; evaluate on test data only once.
mistakes: Tuning on the training set (always favours the highest order).

q: What is stupid backoff and why use it?
short: If the n-gram was seen use its relative frequency; otherwise 0.4 × the score of the (n−1)-gram, recursively. Scores aren't normalised, but it is cheap and works well with web-scale data.
follow: Can you compute perplexity with it?

q: How do you handle unknown words?
short: Choose a vocabulary (count threshold or top-k), replace other training words with <UNK>, estimate its probability like any word, and map test OOV words to <UNK>. Compare perplexities only with the same vocabulary.
detail: Subword tokenisation is the modern answer.

q: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evaluation of LMs?
short: Extrinsic plugs the LM into a task (speech, MT) and measures task accuracy: the true test but expensive. Intrinsic measures perplexity on held-out text: cheap but only correlates with task gains.
detail: Use intrinsic for iteration, extrinsic to confirm.
mistakes: Reporting only perplexity for a product decision.

q: Show that ten equally likely digits give perplexity 10.
short: P(W) = (1/10)^N, so PP = ((1/10)^N)^(−1/N) = 10, independent of N: the model chooses among 10 options per step.
example: If one digit is far more likely, PP drops below 10.

q: Why does a trigram model beat a bigram on newspaper text (109 vs 170) yet can be worse on small data?
short: More context sharpens predictions when counts are reliable; on small data most trigrams are unseen or singletons, so without good smoothing the model overfits and test perplexity rises.
example: Generated trigram text copies training sentences.

q: Explain the idea behind Kneser–Ney smoothing.
short: Subtract a fixed discount d from seen counts (absolute discounting) and give the freed mass to a continuation probability: how many distinct contexts a word follows, so 'Francisco' (frequent but only after 'San') gets a low lower-order weight.
detail: Interpolated KN is the strongest classic n-gram method.
example: 'I can't see without my reading ___' → glasses, not Francisco.
follow: Why is it better than add-k?
mistakes: Using raw unigram frequency for the lower order.

q: Relate perplexity to cross-entropy and to neural LM training.
short: log₂ PP = cross-entropy in bits per word, −(1/N) Σ log₂ P(wᵢ | history). Neural LMs minimise the same cross-entropy (next-token loss), so their validation loss is log perplexity.

q: Build a next-word suggestion feature for a messaging app with an n-gram model.
short: Collect consented text, normalise and tokenise, fix a vocabulary with <UNK>, train interpolated (or Kneser–Ney) trigrams, prune rare n-grams for memory, adapt with a small per-user model interpolated with the global one, evaluate perplexity and keystroke savings, and filter offensive suggestions.
follow: When switch to a neural model?
mistakes: Ignoring memory limits on the device.

q: What can go wrong when comparing perplexities?
short: Different vocabularies or <UNK> handling, different tokenisation (subwords vs words), test data leaking into training, different test domains, and unnormalised scores (stupid backoff) all make numbers incomparable.
detail: Fix vocabulary and test set first.
mistakes: Comparing a model's PP on its own training text.
